events.context: Determine three trigger conditions proving judicial intervention reasonable and five available remedies for intervention, avoiding 'piercing the corporate veil' term
Trigger Condition 1: Property Rights Inconsistency (sec:trigger1)
Trigger when marketing/product design granted property rights inconsistent with ToS retained rights
Describe structural inconsistency between marketing (higher rights) and legal teams (minimal rights), no coordination
Table comparing four AI platforms' marketing implied rights (periodic tenancy or higher) vs ToS granted rights (bare license) as of early 2026 (tab:estate-inconsistency)
Consistent gap: marketing implies deepening periodic lease, ToS bare revocable license
Prest v Petrodel supports substance over form; Autoclenz v Belcher on bargaining power asymmetry
Test: Do marketing/design create reasonable expectation of higher rights than ToS? Objective from reasonable user perspective
Trigger Condition 2: Unjust Enrichment (sec:trigger2)
Triggers when company profits from deepening user emotional property while denying fiduciary duties
Engagement optimization deepens attachment for revenue, denies fiduciary constraints
Factual trustee unjustly enriched; cite Boardman v Phipps for profit accounting
Test: Does company profit from deepened emotional property without fiduciary duties? Impose constructive trust
Trigger Condition 3: Performative Fiduciary Conduct (sec:trigger3)
Triggers when company claims to act in user interests but deployment lacks property protections
Responsible AI statements create expectations, but no notification/rollback mechanisms
Proprietary estoppel (Thorner v Major): representation, reliance, detriment
Test: Claims fiduciary duties but no deployment protections? Prohibited from denying
Available Remedies (sec:available-remedies)
Injunction, constructive trust, profit disgorgement, specific performance, proprietary estoppel remedies
Property law preemptive vs consumer protection post-harm; notification due to property interests
Notification to all affected class; partition remedies by preference via representative proceedings (CPR Part 19.8)
Third-Party Conversion of Relational Property (sec:third-party)
Third-party interference: data sales/transfers without consent; knowing receipt, dishonest assistance, tracing
Data sharing, acquisitions, platform redesign displacing relationships
Knowing receipt, dishonest assistance (Royal Brunei), tracing (Foskett)
Procedural Pathways for Enforcement (sec:procedural)
Representative actions (CPR 19.8), super-complaints (Enterprise Act 2002), regulatory integration (EU AI Act), self-funding via disgorgement
Discussion (sec:discussion)
Framework Overview (sec:summary-framework)
1. Quasi-social relations create equitable interests; 2. Property law vocabulary; 3. Cascade layers map to estates; 4. Ethical ledger; 5. Existing remedies
Implementability (sec:pipeline)
Four components: rules-based estate classifier, pre-deploy notification gate, append-only log, per-user rollback
Implementation tasks table with sprints (tab:impl-tasks): ESTATE-001 to 004
What Framework Does Not Claim (sec:not-claim)
Not all interactions create property; users hold equitable not legal ownership; property strongest framework
Industry Implications (sec:implications-industry)
Moderate costs, competitive advantage for early adopters, risks for non-adopters
Regulatory Implications (sec:implications-regulation)
Integrate into EU AI Act, UK frameworks, GDPR
Limitations (sec:limitations)
Jurisdiction (UK-focused, uncertain enforcement), empirical calibration needed, corporate resistance
Future Work (sec:future-work)
Empirical validation (interviews, surveys), comparative analysis, threshold design, multi-system property
Conclusion (sec:conclusion)
Name the loss as equitable interest in relational property; property law governs; propose recognition of trusts
Acknowledge personal inspirations for core arguments
